title: Components, JSX, and Props
summary: Read and write typed function components: the JSX they return, props and children, and wrappers that forward native props.
intro: Nearly every ticket on a React team touches a component: a card that needs one more field, a new button variant, a message for an empty list. This course reads Taskboard, a team task tracker written in React 19 and TypeScript 7 the way strong teams write apps today. In this lesson you learn to read its building blocks: components, the JSX they return, and the props that configure them.

steps.title: Components and JSX
steps.body:
A component is a function that returns JSX, and its name starts with a capital letter, because a lowercase tag like `
` means an HTML element. JSX looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript calls, so a few names change: `className` instead of `class`, `htmlFor` instead of `for`, and camelCase events like `onClick`. Every tag is closed, and a component returns one root element, or several wrapped in a fragment, `<>...`. Curly braces hold any JavaScript expression: `{task.title}`, `{count + 1}`, or another element. `null`, `undefined`, `true`, and `false` render nothing, which is why `{error &&

{error}

}` is the usual way to show something only when it exists. The number `0` does render, so write `{count > 0 && ...}`, not `{count && ...}`. Rendering must be pure: the same props give the same JSX, and a render never changes anything outside itself. In development, `` renders every component twice to expose the ones that do.

examples.title: A small component
examples.prompt: Read `EmptyState`, which every list in the app shows when it has nothing in it. Notice what renders when `children` or `action` is missing.
examples.explanation:
The props are typed with an interface, so TypeScript checks every place that renders `EmptyState`. `children` and `action` are optional and typed `ReactNode`, the type of anything React can render: text, elements, arrays, or `null`. `{children &&

...

}` renders the paragraph only when there is text, and `{action}` renders the button the caller passed, or nothing. `styles.title` comes from a CSS Module, a stylesheet whose class names are scoped to this one file. `data-ui` is a plain attribute that tests and the design system can find.

examples.title: Where rendering starts
examples.prompt: Read the entry point, which mounts the whole app into the page once.
examples.explanation: `index.html` has an empty `<div id="root">`, and `createRoot` takes it over. The `!` tells TypeScript the element exists. `render` mounts the tree once, and from then on React updates only what changes. `<StrictMode>` does nothing in production. In development it renders twice and runs effects twice, so a missing cleanup shows up on your machine instead of in a bug report. `AppProviders` and `RouterProvider` are components too: they wrap every page in the query cache, the toasts, the theme, and the router. The root's `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` options are where a team plugs in error reporting.

steps.title: Props and children
steps.body:
Props are the one object a component receives. Destructure them in the parameter list and type them with an `interface` or a `type`. Mark optional props with `?` and give them defaults in the destructuring, like `tone = "neutral"`. TypeScript then checks every call: a misspelled prop or a wrong value is a red squiggle, not a bug in production.

`children` is whatever sits between a component's opening and closing tags, typed `ReactNode`. Other props can carry JSX too, like `action={<Button>Create a project</Button>}`.

Props are read-only. A component never changes them: to show something different, the parent renders it again with new props. A prop can be any value: a string, a whole `task` object, a function like `onClose`, or JSX. Name callback props `onSomething`, like DOM events, and the handlers inside a component `handleSomething`.

A wrapper around a native element should accept every prop of that element and pass the ones it doesn't use through. `ComponentProps<"button">` is the type of every prop a `<button>` takes.

examples.title: A typed Tag
examples.prompt: Read `Tag`, the colored label for priorities and task labels. Look at how its props are typed and defaulted.
examples.explanation: `TagTone` is a union of five strings, so `<Tag tone="red">` doesn't compile, and the editor suggests the five values as you type. `tone` defaults to `"neutral"` in the destructuring, and `color` is optional. `children` is required here: a tag with no text makes no sense, and TypeScript says so at the call. `style` takes an object, not a string. A CSS custom property like `--tag-color` isn't in React's style type, hence the `as CSSProperties`. `clsx` joins class names and skips the falsy ones, so `color && styles.custom` adds the class only when there's a color.

examples.title: The parent decides
examples.prompt: Read how `TaskCard` takes a whole task and renders parts of it only when they apply. The board decides `canDelete` and passes it in.
examples.explanation: The card receives a whole `Task`, typed in `types.ts`, instead of a dozen separate props, so adding a field to tasks doesn't change every call site. `assignee` is `Member | undefined`, and the ternary renders an avatar or the word Unassigned. TypeScript won't let you read `assignee.name` without that check. `canDelete` is a decision the parent makes, because only the board knows whether you own the project. The card just renders what it's told, which keeps it easy to reuse and to test. `DueDate` is a second, smaller component in the same file, with an early `return` for tasks that are done.

examples.title: Forwarding native props
examples.prompt: Read `Button`, the app's only styled button. It adds two props of its own and forwards everything else to the real `<button>`.
examples.explanation: `ComponentProps<"button">` is every prop a `<button>` accepts: `onClick`, `disabled`, `aria-label`, `children`, and the rest. The `&` adds `variant` and `size`. The destructuring pulls out what `Button` handles itself and collects everything else in `props`, which `{...props}` passes through, so `<Button disabled={isPending} onClick={save}>Save</Button>` works with no extra code. `type` defaults to `"button"` because a button inside a form submits it by default, a classic bug. `className` is merged with `clsx`, not replaced. Features never style a raw button, so a design change happens here, once.

recap:
- A component is a capitalized function that returns JSX. Lowercase tags are HTML elements.
- JSX uses `className`, `htmlFor`, and camelCase events, and `{}` holds any expression. `null`, `undefined`, and booleans render nothing, but `0` renders.
- Type props with an interface, give defaults in the destructuring, and pass JSX through `children` or other `ReactNode` props.
- Props are read-only: the parent decides, and the child renders what it's given.
- Wrap native elements with `ComponentProps<"button">` and a rest spread, and default `type` to `"button"`.
